theme: Doctrinal Pause: The Nature of the Church
summary: The church as the people of God, body of Christ, temple of the Spirit; visible and invisible; one, holy, catholic, apostolic
readingInstruction: Read Matthew 16:13-20, Ephesians 2:11-22, and 1 Peter 2:4-10. Today is a doctrinal pause on the nature of the church. Notice the images used: a rock, a household, a temple, a priesthood, and a people.
settingTheScene: The word “church” translates the Greek ekklesia, which means an assembly or gathering. In the Old Testament, it was used for the assembly of Israel. Jesus used the word only twice in the Gospels (Matthew 16:18 and 18:17), but in the rest of the New Testament it appears over a hundred times. The church is central to God’s plan. It is not a human invention but the people whom God has gathered to himself through Christ.
observation: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16).
“On this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18).
“But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13).
“For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one” (Ephesians 2:14).
“You are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19).
“You yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood” (1 Peter 2:5).
“But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession” (1 Peter 2:9).
doctrinalFocus:
The church is the people of God, called out of the world by the gospel and united to Christ by the Spirit. It is described in many ways: the body of Christ, the bride of Christ, the household and family of God, the temple of the Spirit, the flock of the Good Shepherd, the pillar and buttress of truth, and the people of God. Each image teaches something. The body speaks of union and mutual dependence; the bride, of love and purity; the family, of belonging; the temple, of God’s presence; the flock, of care.

We can distinguish the universal church and the local church. The universal church is all those united to Christ by faith in every time and place. The local church is a particular gathering of believers who meet regularly under the word, practice the ordinances, and are accountable to each other. Many theologians distinguish the visible church, which includes everyone who professes faith, from the invisible church, which includes only those who are truly regenerate. The marks of a true church, according to the Reformers, are the faithful preaching of the word and the right administration of the sacraments or ordinances. Many add discipline.

The church is what Israel was called to be, now expanded to include Gentiles. In Ephesians 2, Paul says that Gentiles who were “alienated from the commonwealth of Israel” are now fellow citizens. In 1 Peter 2:9, the titles once given to Israel in Exodus 19:5-6 are given to the church: a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation. This is part of the progressive covenantal reading of Scripture: Christ is the true Israel, and the church, united to him, is the people of God, in continuity with the Old Testament people and yet new.

Christians differ on the meaning of “on this rock” in Matthew 16:18. Roman Catholics hold that the rock is Peter, as the first pope. Many Protestants hold that the rock is Peter’s confession (that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God), or Christ himself, or Peter as representative of the apostles. Christians also differ on church government, which we study on Day 811. All agree that Christ builds his church and that it will not fail.
interpretation:
At Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks, “Who do you say that I am?” Peter answers, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Jesus blesses him: flesh and blood did not reveal this, but the Father. “And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” The church is built on the apostolic confession of who Jesus is. Whether the “rock” is Peter, his confession, or both, the point is clear: Christ is the builder, and the gates of death will not stop him. Jesus also gives the keys of the kingdom, the authority to declare, through the gospel, who enters.

Ephesians 2:11-22 describes the church as a new humanity. Gentiles were “separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world.” But now they have been brought near. Christ “has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” between Jew and Gentile, by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, “that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two.” Together they have access in one Spirit to the Father. “So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and the prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone, in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord.” The church is a building with Christ at its center and a living organism that is growing.

Peter adds that believers are “living stones” built into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood to offer spiritual sacrifices. Christ is the living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious. For those who believe, he is precious; for those who do not, he is a stone of stumbling. Believers have a purpose: “that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.” “Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.”

The church is the community of the redeemed. It is not optional for the Christian. We were saved into a people.
connection: Exodus 19:5-6 is the source of 1 Peter 2:9. Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 28:16 are quoted in 1 Peter 2:6-8. Hosea 1:9 to 2:23 is echoed in 1 Peter 2:10. Matthew 18:15-20 gives Jesus’ words on the church. Acts 2:42-47 shows the first church. 1 Corinthians 12:12-27 describes the body. Hebrews 10:24-25 urges us not to neglect meeting together. Revelation 21:9-14 pictures the bride and the city. Ephesians 5:25-27 says Christ loved the church and gave himself for her.
application:
If you are not part of a local church, prayerfully find one this week. If you are, thank God for it.

Ask what it would mean to see your fellow members as brothers and sisters, not as an audience.

Think of the church’s mission: to proclaim the excellencies of him who called us.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for building his church.
Ask him to show you your place in it.
